courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: The Lorentz force law states that the total electromagnetic force on a point charge is F = qE + q(v cross B) = q(E + v cross B), the two terms being added as vectors and never as numbers, with F in newtons, q in coulombs including its sign, E in N/C (equivalently V/m), v in m/s and B in tesla.

The magnetic term has magnitude F = q*v*B*sin(theta) with theta the angle between v and B, so it vanishes both for a charge at rest and for a charge moving parallel or antiparallel to the field and is greatest when v is perpendicular to B; its direction is given by right-hand rule 1 (thumb along v, fingers along B, force out of the palm) for a positive charge and is reversed for a negative one, and it is always perpendicular to the plane containing v and B.

Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant its power F.v is exactly zero, so a magnetic field can bend a charged particle's path but can never change its speed or kinetic energy; only the electric term qE does work, which is why in every accelerator E accelerates and B steers.

In a uniform field a charge with v perpendicular to B moves in a circle of radius r = m*v/(qB) with period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) and cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2*pi*m) that are independent of the speed, while a velocity component along B is untouched and turns the path into a helix of pitch v_parallel*T; crossed electric and magnetic fields transmit undeflected exactly one speed, v = E/B, independent of both charge and mass.

Summing the single-charge law over the moving charges in a conductor, with dq = lambda*dl and I = lambda*v, gives dF = I dl cross B and hence F = I L cross B with magnitude F = B*I*L*sin(theta) for a straight wire in a uniform field, theta being the angle between the current and the field; this is the origin of the torque on a current loop, of the electric motor and of magnetic levitation, and the deck's factors of 1/c belong to Gaussian cgs units and must be dropped in SI.

The week's summary sheet adds electromagnetic oscillations and waves: oscillating electric and magnetic fields sustain one another, are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (which is the direction of E cross B), travel in vacuum at c = 3.00x10^8 m/s so that c = f*lambda, span the spectrum from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma rays in order of increasing frequency, and carry energy h*f per photon.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals: (integral from a to infinity of f) = lim as t -> infinity of (integral from a to t of f), and it converges precisely when that limit exists and is finite, so divergence covers both an infinite limit and a limit that fails to exist because of oscillation.

Type I improper integrals have an infinite interval of integration with a continuous integrand, and a doubly infinite integral (from -infinity to infinity) must be split at some interior point c with both halves required to converge separately, which is why the symmetric Cauchy principal value is not an acceptable evaluation.

Type II improper integrals have a finite interval but an integrand with an infinite discontinuity at an endpoint or, more dangerously, at an interior point, where the Fundamental Theorem may not be applied across the singularity and the integral must be split into two one-sided limits.

The two p-tests point in opposite directions: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^p) converges if and only if p > 1 with value 1/(p-1), while (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^p) converges if and only if p < 1 with value 1/(1-p), and p = 1 diverges at both ends.

The Comparison Test states that if 0 <= f(x) <= g(x) on [a, infinity) then convergence of (integral of g) forces convergence of (integral of f), and divergence of (integral of f) forces divergence of (integral of g); the other two pairings give no information whatsoever, and the non-negativity hypothesis is what makes the truncated integral increasing and therefore convergent once it is bounded above.

The Limit Comparison Test settles cases where the direct inequality points the wrong way: for positive f and g with lim as x -> infinity of f/g = L and 0 < L < infinity, the two integrals converge or diverge together, the comparison function being obtained by keeping only the dominant terms of numerator and denominator.

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: A simple statement contains only one expression and ends with a semicolon, so more than one statement may sit on a single line and one statement may span several lines; a block, or compound statement, contains more than one statement inside curly brackets, takes no semicolon after its right curly bracket, and is treated by the computer like a single statement, which is exactly what allows it to be used wherever one statement is expected.

Blocks exist so that a complex problem broken into smaller ones can have each solution treated as a single unit, and the course names their three applications as functions, decision making statements (if, if-else, if-else-if) and iterative statements (for, while, do-while).

Booleans represent values that are either true or false, and in C a Boolean variable is declared with the bool keyword; but Boolean values are returned as integers, with 1 or any other number that is not 0 representing true and 0 representing false, so truth in C is the numeric property of being nonzero and an if compares its expression with zero rather than with true.

A Boolean expression is built by comparing values and variables with the relational operators ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and combining the results with the logical operators &&, || and !; it evaluates to the integer 1 or 0, its operators obey a fixed precedence in which ! binds tighter than relational, relational tighter than equality, equality tighter than &&, && tighter than || and assignment lowest of all, and && and || short-circuit so that the right operand and all of its side effects are skipped once the left operand settles the result.

Programme control is responsible for the sequential execution of a programme from one line to the next until the last line, and branching means the computer can decide to move program control to another line instead: unconditional branching, whose example is goto, moves control without checking any condition, while conditional branching, also called decision making or selection, moves control only if predetermined conditions are satisfied and comprises if, if-else, if-else-if and switch.

Iteration repeats a block: a while loop tests its condition before the body and so may run zero times, a do-while tests after the body and is guaranteed to execute at least one time, and a for loop executes its init step first and only once, then evaluates the condition, then runs the body, then the increment, before testing again - which is why a for control variable holds the first failing value after the loop ends and why i <= n runs one pass more than i < n.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Specific heat capacity is defined as the heat energy required to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a material by one degree Celsius, has the SI unit J/kgK (equivalently J/kg degC), is a property of the material rather than of the sample, and obeys Q = m*c*(T_f - T_i) with Q positive when the body gains heat.

The specific heat of a solid is determined by the method of mixtures: a block of mass m_s heated on a hot plate to T_s (set between 90 and 99 degC) is transferred with crucible tongs into a calorimeter of mass m_c holding water of mass m_w, both initially at room temperature T_r, and the mixture is allowed to reach a single equilibrium temperature T_f.

The working equation is the principle of conservation of energy applied to the mixture, heat lost by the solid equals heat gained by the water and the calorimeter: m_s*c_s*(T_s - T_f) = (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r), so c_s = (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r) / [m_s*(T_s - T_f)], with c_w = 4186 J/kgK for water and c_c = 387 J/kgK for the copper calorimeter.

The calorimeter term m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c is the total heat capacity of the mixture in J/degC (its water equivalent is that figure divided by c_w); omitting m_c*c_c understates the heat gained and drives the computed specific heat too low, as do heat lost by the block during transfer and heat leaking out of the insulating jacket.

On the deck's own copper data (m_s = 8.9 g, m_c = 36.36 g, m_w = 68.63 g, T_r = 16.1 degC, T_s = 91.3 degC, T_f = 17.0 degC) the heat capacity of water plus calorimeter is 301 J/degC, the heat gained is 271 J and c_s = 410 J/kgK, about 6 percent above copper's accepted 387 J/kgK, the error being dominated by the mere 0.9 degC rise read on a 0.1 degC thermometer.

Repeating the run and plotting the heat gained, (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r), against m_s*(T_s - T_f) gives a straight line through the origin whose gradient is the specific heat of the solid c_s in J/kgK, a non-zero intercept signalling heat lost in transfer or through the jacket.

checks.topic: The concepts of improper integration: the limit definition of convergence and divergence, the distinction between Type I (infinite interval) and Type II (infinite integrand) including interior singularities, the two opposed p-tests and why the same exponent gives opposite verdicts at 0 and at infinity, the exact hypotheses of the Comparison Test and why non-negativity is the hypothesis that makes the argument work, the two pairings of f and g that carry no information, the degenerate cases L = 0 and L = infinity in limit comparison, and how the shape of an integrand decides whether it is evaluated directly or merely tested.

questions.q: To say that (integral from a to infinity of f(x) dx) CONVERGES means precisely that:
options: f(x) -> 0 as x -> infinity
(integral from a to t of f(x) dx) is a finite number for every finite t > a
lim as t -> infinity of (integral from a to t of f(x) dx) exists and is finite
f is bounded on [a, infinity), so the region under the curve has finite height
questions.concept: An improper integral is defined as a limit; convergence is the assertion that this limit exists and is finite.
questions.why: Key (c) is the definition itself. (a) is a condition on the integrand, not the integral, and is neither sufficient (1/x -> 0 yet its integral diverges) nor, for integrals, even necessary. (b) is true for every improper integral of a continuous function, since each truncation is an ordinary Riemann integral, so it says nothing and cannot be a definition. (d) confuses a bounded integrand with a finite integral: 1/x is bounded on [1, infinity) and its integral is infinite.

questions.q: Which of these is an improper integral of Type II?
options: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^2)
(integral from 0 to 1 of dx/(x - 2))
(integral from 1 to 3 of dx/sqrt(x - 1))
(integral from -infinity to 0 of e^x dx)
questions.concept: Type II means the integrand becomes infinite on a finite interval.
questions.why: Key (c): 1/sqrt(x - 1) -> infinity as x -> 1 from the right, and [1, 3] is finite, so it is Type II with an endpoint singularity. (a) and (d) have infinite intervals and continuous integrands, so both are Type I. (b) is the trap: x - 2 vanishes at x = 2, which lies OUTSIDE [0, 1], so the integrand is continuous throughout and the integral is entirely proper. Reading a denominator without checking whether its zero lies inside the interval is the standard misclassification.

questions.q: Exactly one of the following converges. Which?
options: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/sqrt(x))
(integral from 0 to 1 of dx/sqrt(x))
(integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x)
(integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^2)
questions.concept: The p-test near a singularity is the mirror image of the p-test at infinity.
questions.why: Key (b): p = 1/2 < 1 at the origin, so it converges, to 1/(1 - p) = 2. (a) is the same exponent at infinity, where convergence needs p > 1, so it diverges. (c) is p = 1, the boundary case, divergent at either end. (d) is p = 2 near zero, where a large exponent is fatal because the integrand blows up too fast; note that the same p = 2 converges at infinity. Options (a) and (d) are exactly the two exponents applied at the wrong end.

questions.q: On [1, infinity) you have verified that 0 <= f(x) <= g(x), and you know (integral from 1 to infinity of f) CONVERGES. What follows about (integral from 1 to infinity of g)?
options: it converges, to a value at least as large
it diverges, since g is the larger function
it converges, but the comparison test gives no bound on its value
nothing at all follows
questions.concept: Smaller than convergent proves convergence; convergent below proves nothing above.
questions.why: Key (d): the test runs one way only, bounding a function ABOVE by an integrable one. Both outcomes really occur: 1/x^2 <= 1/x^2 gives a convergent g, while 1/x^2 <= 1/x gives a divergent g, with the same convergent f. (a) is the false converse. (b) mistakes 'larger at each point' for 'large enough to diverge', but pointwise size says nothing about the total tail. (c) hides the same false converse behind a caveat about values.

questions.q: The Comparison Test requires 0 <= f(x) <= g(x), not merely f(x) <= g(x). The reason the LOWER bound is needed is that:
options: an integral of a negative function is undefined
f >= 0 makes F(t) = (integral from a to t of f) increasing in t, so bounding it above forces it to have a finite limit
without it the inequality f <= g could reverse for large x
without it the answer would be a principal value rather than an integral
questions.concept: Non-negativity is what converts 'bounded above' into 'convergent'.
questions.why: Key (b) is the entire proof: F is non-decreasing because f >= 0, and bounded above by (integral of g), and an increasing function bounded above must approach a finite limit. (a) is false, since (integral from 1 to infinity of -1/x^2 dx) = -1 is perfectly well defined. (c) is not a consequence of dropping f >= 0; the inequality is assumed to hold throughout regardless of sign. (d) confuses this hypothesis with the separate matter of splitting a doubly infinite integral. For sign-changing f the repair is to compare |f| with g and invoke absolute convergence.

questions.q: For (integral from 0 to 3 of dx/(x - 1)^2) the correct first step is to:
options: write [-1/(x - 1)] evaluated from 0 to 3 and obtain -3/2
note that the interval is finite and the integral is therefore proper
split the integral at x = 1 and take a one-sided limit into x = 1 from each side
compare the integrand with 1/x^2 on [0, 3]
questions.concept: An infinite discontinuity strictly inside the interval makes the integral Type II there, and the Fundamental Theorem does not apply across it.
questions.why: Key (c): the integrand blows up at x = 1, which lies in (0, 3), so the integral is the sum of two one-sided limits, and here both are +infinity. (a) applies the Fundamental Theorem to an antiderivative that is discontinuous on the interval and returns -3/2, a negative number for a strictly positive integrand, which is the built-in absurdity that should catch it. (b) checks only the interval and ignores the integrand, which is precisely what Type II is about. (d) is a plausible-sounding but useless move: the trouble is at x = 1, not at infinity, and 1/x^2 is itself unbounded at 0.

questions.q: f and g are positive and continuous on [1, infinity), lim as x -> infinity of f(x)/g(x) = 0, and (integral from 1 to infinity of g) converges. Then (integral from 1 to infinity of f):
options: converges, because f is eventually smaller than g
diverges, because a ratio tending to 0 means f is negligible and the test does not apply
may converge or diverge, since the Limit Comparison Test needs 0 < L < infinity so nothing can be said
converges only if in addition f(x) -> 0 as x -> infinity
questions.concept: L = 0 gives a one-way conclusion, and here it is the useful direction.
questions.why: Key (a): f/g -> 0 means that eventually f(x) < g(x), so f is dominated by an integrable function and the ordinary Comparison Test applies. (c) is the most attractive wrong answer: it correctly recalls that the TWO-WAY conclusion needs 0 < L < infinity, but forgets that each degenerate case still yields one implication (L = 0: g convergent implies f convergent; L = infinity: g divergent implies f divergent). (b) treats negligibility as a reason to abandon the test when it is exactly what makes it work. (d) adds a condition that is neither necessary nor sufficient.

questions.q: To decide (integral from 2 to infinity of (3x + 5)/(x^3 + x) dx) the natural comparison function is:
options: 1/x, because the numerator has degree 1
1/x^2, because for large x the integrand behaves like 3x/x^3
1/x^3, because the denominator has degree 3
1/x^4, because a comparison proving convergence needs a smaller function
questions.concept: Comparison is decided by order of growth, obtained by keeping only the leading terms.
questions.why: Key (b): (3x + 5)/(x^3 + x) behaves like 3x/x^3 = 3/x^2, so the comparison function is 1/x^2 (p = 2 > 1, convergent) and the constant 3 is irrelevant. (a) reads only the numerator and (c) only the denominator; both ignore that it is the DIFFERENCE of degrees, 3 - 1 = 2, that fixes the exponent. (d) inverts the logic of the test: proving convergence needs an upper bound, so a smaller comparison function is exactly the useless direction.

questions.q: (explain why) (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^p) converges exactly when p > 1, while (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^p) converges exactly when p < 1. Derive both statements from the same antiderivative and explain in words why the condition reverses.
questions.concept: Both p-tests come from the single antiderivative x^(1-p)/(1-p); which end is dangerous depends on whether the exponent 1 - p drives that power to 0 or to infinity.
questions.why: For p not equal to 1, (integral of dx/x^p) = x^(1-p)/(1-p). At infinity: (integral from 1 to t) = (t^(1-p) - 1)/(1-p); if p > 1 then 1 - p < 0 so t^(1-p) -> 0 and the limit is 1/(p-1), finite, hence convergent; if p < 1 then 1 - p > 0 so t^(1-p) -> infinity and it diverges. At zero: (integral from t to 1) = (1 - t^(1-p))/(1-p); if p < 1 then t^(1-p) -> 0 and the limit is 1/(1-p), convergent; if p > 1 then t^(1-p) -> infinity and it diverges. The case p = 1 is handled separately by ln and diverges at both ends. In words: at infinity the enemy is a tail that decays too slowly, so you need the integrand to shrink fast, that is large p; near zero the enemy is a spike that grows too fast, so you need the integrand to blow up gently, that is small p. The same exponent that makes 1/x^2 safe far away makes it fatal near 0, and p = 1 is the exact dividing line that fails on both sides.

questions.q: (explain why) A student writes: '1/(x ln x) < 1/x on [2, infinity), and (integral from 2 to infinity of dx/x) diverges, therefore (integral from 2 to infinity of dx/(x ln x)) diverges.' State exactly which hypothesis of the Comparison Test this argument violates, and give two integrands both smaller than 1/x on [2, infinity) that behave differently, to show the reasoning can never be repaired.
questions.concept: The Comparison Test concludes only from 'smaller than convergent' and 'bigger than divergent'; being smaller than a divergent function is one of the two combinations that carry no information.
questions.why: The argument uses f <= g with (integral of g) divergent and concludes that (integral of f) diverges, but the divergence half of the test runs the other way: it needs the SMALLER function to diverge in order to conclude that the larger one does. Here 1/(x ln x) is the smaller function and 1/x the larger, so the hypothesis '(integral of the smaller) diverges' was never established and nothing follows. That it can never be repaired is shown by two integrands both lying under 1/x on [2, infinity) with opposite behaviour: (integral from 2 to infinity of dx/(x ln x)) = lim of [ln ln x] from 2 to t = infinity, divergent, while (integral from 2 to infinity of dx/(x (ln x)^2)) = lim of [-1/ln x] from 2 to t = 1/ln 2, convergent. Since the same hypothesis holds for both, no valid theorem can draw a conclusion from it. Incidentally the student's verdict for 1/(x ln x) is correct, but the reasoning is invalid, and in an examination the reasoning is what is marked.

questions.q: (explain why) Explain why (integral from -infinity to infinity of f(x) dx) must be split at some point c with both halves required to converge separately, and why lim as t -> infinity of (integral from -t to t of 2x/(1 + x^2) dx) = 0 is NOT an evaluation of (integral from -infinity to infinity of 2x/(1 + x^2) dx).
questions.concept: A doubly infinite integral is defined as the sum of two independent limits, and a single symmetric limit is a different object, the Cauchy principal value.
questions.why: By definition (integral from -infinity to infinity of f) = (integral from -infinity to c of f) + (integral from c to infinity of f) for any convenient c, with EACH piece required to converge on its own; the choice of c is immaterial because moving it changes each piece by the same finite amount. Both halves are required so that the value does not depend on how the two infinities are approached: if one half were +infinity and the other -infinity, different rates of approach would give different answers and no single value could be assigned. For 2x/(1 + x^2): (integral from 0 to t) = ln(1 + t^2) -> infinity, so the right half diverges and therefore the whole integral diverges. The symmetric limit is 0 only because the odd integrand makes the two halves cancel at exactly the same rate; take (integral from -t to 2t) instead and you get ln(1 + 4t^2) - ln(1 + t^2) -> ln 4. That the answer depends on the route is exactly why the symmetric value is called the principal value and is not accepted as the integral.

questions.q: (explain why) For each of (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/(x^2 + 3)), (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/(1 - x)) and (integral from 1 to infinity of (sin x)^2/x^2 dx): say whether it is Type I, Type II or both, and say whether you would settle it by direct evaluation or by comparison, naming the feature of the integrand that decides. Do not evaluate anything.
questions.concept: Type is decided by where the trouble is (infinite interval, infinite integrand, or both), and method is decided by whether an antiderivative is available.
questions.why: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/(x^2 + 3)): Type I only, since the interval is infinite and x^2 + 3 never vanishes, so the integrand is continuous on [1, infinity). Direct evaluation, because a standard antiderivative exists, (1/sqrt(3)) arctan(x/sqrt(3)). (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/(1 - x)): Type II only, since the interval is finite but the denominator vanishes at the upper endpoint x = 1, so the integrand is unbounded there. Direct evaluation by a one-sided limit, since -ln|1 - x| is available, and it diverges. (integral from 1 to infinity of (sin x)^2/x^2 dx): Type I, infinite interval with a continuous integrand throughout, since (sin x)^2 is bounded and there is no singularity. Comparison, because (sin x)^2/x^2 has no elementary antiderivative; the decisive feature is 0 <= (sin x)^2 <= 1, so the integrand lies between 0 and 1/x^2, and (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^2) converges. Note that comparison yields convergence only, not a value.

checks.topic: The Lorentz force as concepts: what each term in F = q(E + v cross B) means and the exact conditions under which each one vanishes, why the magnetic force is perpendicular to both v and B and therefore does no work, the RHR-1 direction rule and what reversing the sign of q changes, why the orbit in a uniform field is a circle or a helix and why its period is independent of speed, how the crossed-field velocity selector works, why F = I L cross B is the single-charge law summed over the moving charges in a wire, and the transverse geometry of an electromagnetic wave

questions.q: The magnetic part of the Lorentz force on a charged particle is found to be zero, although the particle is inside a strong uniform magnetic field. The possible reasons are:
options: the field is uniform, and a uniform field exerts no force on a point charge - only a torque on a dipole
the particle is at rest, or its velocity lies along B; in either case v cross B = 0
the particle's charge is negative, so the minus sign cancels the force
the particle's velocity is perpendicular to B, which is where the sine factor passes through zero
questions.concept: The magnetic force needs motion, and motion across the field
questions.why: F = q*v*B*sin(theta) vanishes in exactly two ways: v = 0, so a stationary charge feels nothing magnetic however strong the field; and sin(theta) = 0, that is v parallel or antiparallel to B, since the cross product of parallel vectors is zero - which is why charged particles spiral along field lines rather than across them. (a) misapplies the Week 8 dipole result to a single moving charge, which a uniform field pushes very hard. (c) confuses a sign with a magnitude: a negative charge feels an equal force in the opposite direction, never none. (d) is the sin/cos inversion - v perpendicular to B is where the force is maximum.

questions.q: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field in such a way that the magnetic force on it is a maximum. It follows that:
options: its velocity is parallel to B, the two vectors reinforcing each other
its velocity is perpendicular to B, and the force is perpendicular to both v and B
its velocity is perpendicular to B, and the force therefore lies along B
its velocity is at 45 degrees to B, the angle that balances the sine and cosine factors
questions.concept: Maximum force at theta = 90 degrees, with F still perpendicular to both vectors
questions.why: sin(theta) peaks at 90 degrees, so the force is greatest when v is perpendicular to B, and F = q*v cross B is then perpendicular to the plane containing them - perpendicular to v, hence no work, and perpendicular to B. (a) has the angle exactly backwards; parallel vectors give zero force. (c) is the sharpest distractor: right angle, wrong direction - v cross B is perpendicular to B by construction and can never lie along it. (d) invents a compromise angle by analogy with projectile range; there is no cosine factor in F = q*v*B*sin(theta) to balance.

questions.q: A magnetic field can steer a charged particle but can never increase its kinetic energy. The reason is that:
options: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so its power F.v is zero at every instant
the magnetic force is far weaker than the electric force at ordinary speeds, so the work it does is negligible
magnetic field lines are closed loops, so any energy gained on one part of the path is given back on another
the magnetic force acts on the particle's spin rather than on its translational motion
questions.concept: F perpendicular to v gives P = F.v = 0 exactly and at every instant
questions.why: Work is the integral of F.dl with dl along v, so a force permanently at right angles to the motion contributes nothing anywhere on the path; speed and kinetic energy are rigorously constant. (b) makes the result a matter of size, which would let a strong enough field do work - it cannot, at any strength. (c) is the most dangerous answer because it nearly argues: it concedes that work is done and claims it cancels round a loop, which would still allow the particle to speed up and slow down within one orbit, and would fail entirely on an unclosed helical path. (d) invents a spin interaction; q*v cross B acts on the translational velocity and the result holds for a spinless particle.

questions.q: A charge enters a uniform magnetic field with velocity components both along and across B, and follows a helix. The helix arises because:
options: the field exerts a force along B that stretches the circular orbit out into a spiral
the component of v along B is never changed, since the force has no component along B, while the perpendicular component is turned in a circle
the field weakens along its own direction, so the radius grows from turn to turn
the particle radiates energy as it circulates, so the closed circle gradually opens out
questions.concept: v cross B has no component along B, so the parallel motion survives untouched
questions.why: F = q*v cross B is perpendicular to B, so it has no component along B: the parallel part of the velocity is never accelerated or retarded and drifts on uniformly, while the perpendicular part feels a constant-magnitude transverse force and is bent into a circle of radius m*v_perp/(qB). Uniform drift plus circle equals helix, of pitch v_parallel * T. (a) asserts a force along B, which the cross product forbids. (c) invents a non-uniform field; in a genuinely converging field the radius would shrink, giving a magnetic mirror. (d) appeals to radiation, negligible here, and the helix appears even in the idealised non-radiating treatment.

questions.q: The period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) of a charged particle's circular orbit does not depend on its speed. This is because:
options: the magnetic force does no work, so no property of the motion can change
a faster particle sweeps a proportionally larger circle, and the extra path length exactly offsets the extra speed
the period is fixed by the field alone, and the field has been specified as uniform
the speed cancels because it enters the centripetal expression squared and the magnetic force once
questions.concept: Circumference and speed are both proportional to v, so they cancel (isochronism)
questions.why: r = m*v_perp/(qB) grows in exact proportion to the speed, so the circumference does too, and T = 2*pi*r/v_perp = 2*pi*m/(qB) has no v in it: a faster particle travels further and proportionately faster, arriving at the same moment - which is what lets a cyclotron run at one fixed frequency. (a) is a true statement used as a non sequitur: no-work fixes the speed of a given particle and says nothing about comparing particles of different speeds. (c) is empty - the field is uniform in both cases, and T also depends on m and q. (d) is a pseudo-derivation: q*v*B = m*v^2/r cancels one power of v, leaving r proportional to v, and the second cancellation happens only on dividing the circumference by the speed.

questions.q: In a velocity selector, one and the same speed passes undeflected for every particle admitted - electrons, protons, heavy ions alike. This is because:
options: both forces are proportional to q, so q cancels, and neither force contains the mass at all
both the electric and the magnetic force are proportional to v, so their ratio is fixed whatever the particle
heavier particles are deflected less, and that compensates exactly for their greater inertia
the field strengths are re-adjusted for each species before its beam is admitted
questions.concept: q cancels from qE = q*v*B and m never appears
questions.why: The balance condition qE = q*v*B divides through by q to give v = E/B - no charge, no sign, no mass; reverse the sign of the charge and both forces reverse together, so the balance survives, which is what makes it a speed filter rather than a species filter. (b) is false about the electric force, which is qE regardless of v - and the whole mechanism depends on that asymmetry, one force depending on speed and the other not, so the two balance at one speed only. (c) invents a mass dependence and then a compensation for it; neither force involves m. (d) describes an apparatus needing constant retuning, which is exactly the labour the selector saves.

questions.q: The force on a current-carrying wire, F = I L cross B, is:
options: an independent law, obtained from Ampere's law rather than from the Lorentz force
the single-charge law q*v cross B summed over the moving charges: dq = lambda*dl and I = lambda*v give dF = I dl cross B
valid only for wires, the Lorentz force being valid only for isolated charges, so the two are logically independent
a consequence of Newton's third law applied between the field and the wire
questions.concept: The wire law is the single-charge law counted per unit length
questions.why: An element dl carrying free charge of linear density lambda drifting at v holds dq = lambda*dl and feels dF = (dq) v cross B = (lambda*dl) v cross B; since I = lambda*v this is dF = I dl cross B, integrating to F = I L cross B with magnitude B*I*L*sin(theta). It is the same physics counted per unit length instead of per particle. (a) confuses the two halves of magnetostatics: Ampere's law says what a current produces, the Lorentz force says what a field does to a current. (c) makes two laws where there is one and leaves no account of why the constants agree. (d) misuses Newton's third law, which relates forces between two currents and cannot by itself yield B*I*L*sin(theta).

questions.q: The deck writes the force on a current element as dF = (I/c) dl cross B. Judged as an SI formula, this expression:
options: is correct, the c being the conversion from amperes to the units in which B is measured
is correct only for relativistic currents, in which the drift speed approaches c
is the cgs (Gaussian) form; in SI the factor 1/c is absent and the law reads dF = I dl cross B
is dimensionally sound in both systems, so either version may be used with SI data
questions.concept: The factor 1/c belongs to Gaussian cgs units, not to SI
questions.why: In Gaussian units the magnetic force is written q(v/c) cross B and the current-element force (I/c) dl cross B, because B is defined so that E and B share dimensions; in SI there is no c, and F = q*v cross B, dF = I dl cross B. Dividing an SI answer by 3x10^8 makes it wrong by that factor. (a) invents a unit conversion for a current measured in amperes on both sides. (b) confuses the drift speed of the charges - under a millimetre per second in copper - with the constant c, which the cgs formula carries whatever the drift speed. (d) is the costliest answer: the two forms are not dimensionally interchangeable, and mixing systems produces answers wrong by eight orders of magnitude.

questions.q: Explain why the magnetic force does no work, and say exactly what is conserved as a result and what is not. Then explain why 'does no work' is not the same as 'exerts no force' and not the same as 'produces no acceleration'. Finish by explaining how a cyclotron nevertheless raises a proton's energy to many MeV.
questions.concept: The no-work property of the magnetic force, and what it does and does not forbid
questions.why: The magnetic force F = q*v cross B is perpendicular to both its factors, in particular perpendicular to v at every instant; work is the integral of F.dl with dl along v, so the integrand is identically zero and the instantaneous power P = F.v = 0. Hence the speed and the kinetic energy are exactly conserved however strong the field and however long the particle stays in it. What is not conserved is the momentum p = m*v, a vector whose direction turns continuously and reverses completely over half a revolution; nor is the velocity. 'Does no work' is not 'exerts no force': there is a real force of magnitude q*v*B, large enough to bend a proton beam round a 27 km ring. It is also not 'produces no acceleration': a = q*v*B/m is real and is what curves the path - a centripetal acceleration that changes the direction of v and not its magnitude, and confusing acceleration with speeding up is the error this topic exposes. A cyclotron therefore never uses the magnetic field to add energy. The field's job is to bend the protons round semicircles inside the dees and, because T = 2*pi*m/(qB) is independent of speed, to return them to the gap at strictly regular intervals. The energy comes entirely from the electric field across that gap: each crossing finds the alternating voltage reversed so that qE accelerates the proton again, adding qV of kinetic energy, and the radius grows as r = m*v/(qB) until after hundreds of crossings the proton spirals out at many MeV. Every joule came from E and none from B.

questions.q: From the two defining properties of the cross product, explain why the magnetic force is zero when v is parallel to B and greatest when v is perpendicular to B, and why the force is perpendicular to both. Then explain what reversing the sign of the charge does, and reconcile these two facts: an electron and a proton fired in the same direction through the same field curve opposite ways, yet an electron beam and a positive-ion beam travelling in opposite directions curve the same way.
questions.concept: The geometry of v cross B and the effect of the sign of q
questions.why: A cross product has two defining properties. Magnitude |v cross B| = v*B*sin(theta), theta being the angle between the vectors: zero when they are parallel or antiparallel (sin(theta) = 0) and greatest when they are perpendicular (sin(theta) = 1). Direction: v cross B is perpendicular to the plane containing v and B, with the sense given by the right hand. Both facts about the magnetic force follow at once - a charge moving along a field line feels nothing and travels straight, a charge moving across the field feels the full q*v*B, and the force is perpendicular to v, which is why it does no work, and perpendicular to B, which is why motion along B is never affected. RHR-1 as the deck states it - thumb along v, fingers along B, force out of the palm - expresses that sense and gives the force on a positive charge. Reversing the sign of q reverses F, because q multiplies the whole vector; for an electron, compute the positive-charge answer and turn it round. The two observations are reconciled by noticing that F depends on the product q*v, not on q or v separately. An electron and a proton fired the same way have opposite q and the same v, so q*v is opposite and the forces are opposite: they curve apart. An electron beam moving one way and a positive-ion beam moving the other have opposite q and opposite v, and the two reversals cancel, so q*v is the same and they curve the same way - which is exactly why a conventional current to the right and an electron flow to the left are the same current and feel the same force.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of the crossed-field velocity selector: why exactly one speed passes undeflected, why that speed is E/B and contains neither the charge nor the mass, what happens to particles faster and slower than the selected speed and which force wins in each case, and how adding a second, magnet-only stage converts the apparatus into a mass spectrometer.
questions.concept: The velocity selector: one speed-dependent force set against one speed-independent force
questions.why: Arrange E and B perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the beam. A particle of charge q and speed v then feels an electric force qE, whose size does not depend on v, and a magnetic force q*v*B, whose size is proportional to v, with the geometry set so that the two oppose. Undeflected passage requires qE = q*v*B, hence v = E/B. Two features carry the physics. First, q cancels, sign included: reversing the charge reverses both forces together, so electrons and positive ions of the same speed both pass. Second, m never appears, since neither force involves the mass. The selected speed is a property of the apparatus, not of the particle. Because one force grows with v and the other does not, the balance holds at exactly one speed: a particle faster than E/B has q*v*B > qE, so the magnetic force wins and deflects it to the side the magnetic force points; a slower particle has q*v*B < qE, so the electric force wins and deflects it the other way. Both miss the exit slit. Passing the surviving beam into a second region containing B alone bends it into a circle of radius r = m*v/(q*B'), and since v is now known and fixed by the first stage, the radius measures m/q directly: heavier ions of the same charge sweep proportionally larger circles. The division of labour is the point - the first stage removes the speed spread that would blur the mass measurement, and the second separates by mass.

questions.q: For a plane electromagnetic wave, explain why E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, and what sustains the wave as it travels. Explain why the frequency and the wavelength are inversely related while the speed is fixed at c, and state what physically distinguishes a gamma ray from a radio wave given that both travel at exactly the same speed.
questions.concept: The transverse geometry of an electromagnetic wave, and c = f*lambda
questions.why: An electromagnetic wave is a self-sustaining pair of oscillating fields: a changing electric field generates a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field generates an electric field, so once launched - for instance by the oscillating current in a transmitting aerial - the disturbance regenerates itself and travels away. The generation is by a cross-product relation, so each field is produced at right angles to the one producing it: hence E perpendicular to B, and both perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is the direction of E cross B. The wave is therefore transverse, with no component of either field along the direction of propagation; the standard wrong picture, with E oscillating back and forth along the line of travel, describes a longitudinal wave such as sound and cannot be electromagnetic at all. The speed in vacuum is fixed by the electric and magnetic properties of free space, c = 3.00x10^8 m/s, and is the same for every electromagnetic wave whatever its frequency. Since the wave advances one wavelength per period, c = f*lambda, and because c is constant, f and lambda are inversely proportional. The only physical difference between a gamma ray and a radio wave is that frequency and what follows from it: both are the same transverse E-B disturbance at the same speed, but the gamma ray has an enormously higher frequency, a correspondingly shorter wavelength, and therefore an enormously larger energy per photon, E = h*f = h*c/lambda - a few MeV against a fraction of a microelectronvolt. That is why gamma rays ionise and radio waves do not, and why radio waves diffract round buildings while gamma rays travel in essentially straight lines.

checks.topic: Boolean expressions and control flow as concepts: simple statements versus blocks and why a block counts as a single statement, what makes a value true in C, what a Boolean expression evaluates to, the truth tables for &&, || and ! with De Morgan's laws, operator precedence, short-circuit evaluation and its effect on side effects, and the exact entry condition and pass count of if, if-else, if-else-if, switch, while, do-while, for and goto.

questions.q: In C, which one of these conditions is FALSE?
options: if ('a')
questions.concept: Truth in C is 'not zero'; falsity is 'exactly zero'.
questions.why: The course's rule is that Boolean values are returned as integers with 1 (or any other number that is not 0) representing true and 0 representing false. 2 - 2 evaluates to 0, the one value that is false. (a) -3 is not 0, so it is true; a negative number is just as true as a positive one, and 'true means positive' is the commonest form of the error. (c) 'a' is a character constant whose value is 97, which is not 0, so it is true. (d) 0.5 is not 0, so it is true; the trap is thinking a value 'between false and true' rounds down to false, when the only test performed is a comparison with zero. Note that none of the four contains a relational operator and all four are still perfectly ordinary conditions.

questions.q: The course says a block is 'treated like a single statement by the computer'. Which consequence follows DIRECTLY from that sentence?
options: That the statements inside a block are executed as one indivisible step, so no other part of the programme can interrupt them part-way through
That the compiler compresses the block into one machine instruction, which is why a block runs faster than the same statements written separately
That a block may be written anywhere a single statement is allowed, which is what lets an if or a while, each of which governs exactly one statement, control several statements at once
That the statements inside a block share one semicolon, which is why the closing curly bracket does not need one of its own
questions.concept: The 'one statement' property is a syntactic fact, and it is what makes braces load-bearing.
questions.why: Constructs such as if, while and for are defined to govern exactly ONE statement. A block is treated like a single statement, so wrapping several statements in curly brackets is the only way to put more than one of them under a condition or inside a loop, which is why the course lists the applications of blocks as functions, decision making statements, and iterative statements. (a) reads 'treated like a single statement' as atomic or uninterruptible, importing an idea from concurrency the course never raises; the statements inside run one after another as they would anywhere else. (b) reads it as a performance claim; the block compiles to the same instructions and grouping is not an optimisation. (d) invents a shared semicolon; each statement keeps its own, and the right curly bracket takes no semicolon because the brace itself closes the block.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to !(a || b)?
options: a && b
!a && b
questions.concept: De Morgan: pushing a ! inside brackets flips the operator as well as negating each operand.
questions.why: 'Not (a or b)' means 'neither' - both must be false - which is !a && !b. (a) negates the operands but leaves the operator, giving the law for !(a && b) instead; the two laws are commonly memorised as one and then applied to the wrong expression. Check a = 1, b = 0: !(1 || 0) is 0, but !1 || !0 is 0 || 1 = 1. (b) drops the negation and swaps the operator arbitrarily; it agrees with the original only when both operands are false. (c) negates one operand only, which cannot be right by symmetry - a and b play the same role in a || b, so they must play the same role in its negation.

questions.q: How does  a == 0 || b == 0 && c == 0  group?
questions.concept: && binds tighter than ||, exactly as * binds tighter than +.
questions.why: Equality forms first (a == 0, b == 0, c == 0), then && joins the last two, then || joins that result to the first. The expression is true if a is 0, OR if b and c are both 0. (b) is the reading of someone who takes || and && to be equal in precedence and left-associative, which would make the expression true only when c is 0 - a completely different condition, and the fault behind 'my check works except when c is nonzero'. (c) treats == as though it bound loosest and chains it, which is not how these operators associate. (d) invents a duplicated operand. The safe habit is to write the brackets of (a) explicitly even though they are not required.

questions.q: check(x) && record(x) is evaluated, and check(x) returns 0. record(x) writes a line to a file and returns 1. What happens?
options: record(x) is still called and still writes its line, but its return value is discarded, because && must have both values before it can produce a result
The compiler rejects the expression, because an operand of && may not be a function call that has an effect outside itself
record(x) is not called at all, so no line is written - a skipped operand's side effects do not happen - and the whole expression is 0
record(x) is not called, but the expression takes the value 1, because an operand that could not be evaluated is treated as true by default
questions.concept: Short-circuit evaluation: a skipped operand is not evaluated, so its side effects do not happen.
questions.why: && evaluates its left operand first; check(x) returns 0, which is false, and no value of the right operand can make 0 && anything come out as anything but 0. The answer is settled, record(x) is never called, nothing is written, and the expression is 0. (a) is the misconception that && is like arithmetic and must collect both operands before combining them; if that were so, the standard guard if (n != 0 && total / n > 5) would divide by zero. (d) invents a default value for an unevaluated operand; there is no value, because there was no evaluation. (b) invents a restriction on what may appear in a condition; calls with effects are legal there, which is exactly why the skipping rule must be known rather than assumed.

questions.q: A loop's condition is already false at the moment control first reaches the loop. Which statement is correct?
options: A while runs its body once and a do-while runs it zero times, since do-while checks the condition before committing to a pass
Both run their bodies zero times, since a false condition means there is nothing to do in either construct
A while runs its body zero times and a do-while runs it once, since a do-while tests the condition after the body and so is guaranteed to execute at least one time
Both run their bodies once, since a loop must always complete one pass before it has anything to test
questions.concept: while tests before the body, do-while after; only do-while is guaranteed to run at least once.
questions.why: The course states it directly: a do-while loop works the same way as a while loop, except the fact that it is guaranteed to execute at least one time. With a condition false from the start, a while evaluates it, finds 0, and passes control to the line immediately following the loop without entering the body; a do-while executes the body first and only then discovers the condition is false, so exactly one pass has happened. (a) has both rules the right way round in the words and the wrong way round on the constructs - the classic swap, and the reason the answer must be reasoned from where the test sits. (b) applies the while rule to both, which would make do-while pointless as a separate construct. (d) applies the do-while rule to both, which would make a zero-pass while impossible and break every loop written to handle an empty list.

questions.q: A programmer replaces  if (n > 100) A; else if (n > 50) B; else C;  with three separate if statements carrying the same three conditions. What has changed?
options: Nothing, provided the conditions are copied exactly, since the same tests are being applied to the same value

In the chain, the conditions are tested top to bottom and the first true one wins, so at most one branch runs; with three separate ifs each condition is tested independently, so n = 200 now runs A and B and C
The chain is faster because it stops testing early, but the three separate ifs produce identical output, so the change is only a matter of efficiency
The three separate ifs can no longer run C, because a bare else is the only construct that can execute when no condition is satisfied
questions.concept: An if-else-if chain stops at the first true condition; separate ifs test every condition independently.
questions.why: In the chain, n = 200 satisfies n > 100, so A runs and n > 50 is never even tested - every later condition is skipped. Rewritten as three separate ifs, all three conditions are evaluated: 200 > 100 is true so A runs, 200 > 50 is also true so B runs, and the third if runs C as well if its condition is true. The chain's later branches are written on the assumption that all earlier conditions failed, and separating them destroys that assumption silently. (a) is the belief that the same conditions must give the same behaviour; what differs is not the conditions but which of them are REACHED. (c) treats the difference as efficiency only, the half-right answer that costs the mark: the early stop is not merely faster, it is what makes the branches exclusive. (d) is wrong about else - a final else can be replaced by an if carrying the negation of the earlier conditions, so C is still reachable, just no longer automatic.

questions.q: Which pair of statements matches the course's definitions of unconditional and conditional branching?
options: Unconditional branching moves program control to a specific statement or block without checking any condition, goto being the example; conditional branching moves it depending on whether some predetermined conditions are satisfied, and its statements are also called decision making or selection statements
Unconditional branching is the normal sequential movement from one line to the next, and conditional branching is any statement that interrupts it
Unconditional branching is performed by loops, because a loop repeats regardless of what any single statement says; conditional branching is performed by if, because only if mentions a condition
Unconditional branching is decided by the compiler before the programme runs, whereas conditional branching is decided while it runs, which is why goto costs nothing at run time
questions.concept: The course's definitions of unconditional and conditional branching.
questions.why: Word for word: unconditional statements can move program control to either a specific statement or block without checking any condition, the example given being goto; with conditional branching, where program control moves to is dependent on if some predetermined conditions are satisfied or not, and such statements are also known as decision making or selection statements. (b) inverts the definition of branching itself: branching means the computer can decide to move program control to another line of code INSTEAD OF the usual movement from one line to the next, so ordinary sequential flow is what branching departs from, not a kind of branching. (c) misassigns the constructs; loops are iterative statements, and goto - not the loop - is the deck's example of an unconditional branch. (d) invents a compile-time / run-time distinction; goto transfers control while the programme runs, and both kinds of branching are run-time behaviour.

questions.q: Explain what a Boolean expression is and state precisely what it EVALUATES TO in C, quoting the course's rule about integers. Then use that rule to explain two separate faults: why if (x = 5) is always true no matter what x held before, and why if (flag == true) is a bug in a programme that sets flag to 2. Say in each case what should have been written.
questions.concept: A Boolean expression is an expression with an integer value, and both '=' and '== true' fail because of what that value is.
questions.why:
WHAT IT IS. An expression whose purpose is to be true or false: typically a comparison of values or variables - the course's point that to make decisions and find answers in programming it is sometimes useful to compare values and variables, and when this comparison activity takes place the return value is usually a Boolean value - combined where necessary with &&, || and !. The six relational operators are ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=.
WHAT IT EVALUATES TO. Not a question and not a special kind of thing: an ordinary INTEGER. The course's rule is that Boolean values are returned as integers, with 1 (or any other number that is not 0) representing true and 0 representing false. So 7 > 3 has the value 1 exactly as 3 + 4 has the value 7; it can be printed with %d, stored in an int, or added to another. An if does one thing only: it evaluates its expression and asks whether the result is zero.
FAULT 1: if (x = 5). '=' is the assignment operator, not the comparison operator. x = 5 stores 5 in x, and the value of the assignment expression is the value assigned, namely 5. Five is not zero, so the condition is TRUE, and it is true regardless of what x held before, because the old value was overwritten before anything was tested. Two things go wrong at once: the branch always runs, and the variable is silently destroyed. It compiles without complaint because an assignment is a perfectly legal expression. Should have been written: if (x == 5).
FAULT 2: if (flag == true). 'true' is the name <stdbool.h> gives to the integer 1, so this compares flag with 1 and nothing more. If flag holds 2, then flag == true is 2 == 1, which is 0, so the branch is skipped even though 2 is a perfectly good true value by the course's own rule. The test has quietly narrowed 'true' from 'not zero' to 'exactly one'. Should have been written: if (flag), and for the negation if (!flag) rather than if (flag == false).
THE PRINCIPLE behind both: an if never compares anything with truth - it compares with zero - so the condition should be written to BE the truth, not to be tested against it.

questions.q: Write out the truth tables for a && b, a || b and !a, using 1 and 0 as C stores them. State each operator's rule in one sentence. Then state both of De Morgan's laws and prove one of them wrong-way-round by naming a single row on which !(a && b) and !a && !b disagree. Finally, explain why 0 < x < 10 is true for EVERY value of x, and what must be written instead.
questions.concept: The truth tables, De Morgan's laws, and why C has no chained comparison.
questions.why:
THE TABLES, in C's own values. a=0,b=0: a&&b = 0, a||b = 0, !a = 1. a=0,b=1: a&&b = 0, a||b = 1, !a = 1. a=1,b=0: a&&b = 0, a||b = 1, !a = 0. a=1,b=1: a&&b = 1, a||b = 1, !a = 0.
THE RULES. && is true only when both operands are true, so a single false operand settles the result. || is false only when both operands are false, so a single true operand settles the result. ! swaps 1 and 0. (The 'single operand settles it' phrasing is the same fact as short-circuit evaluation, seen from the table rather than from the evaluation order.)
DE MORGAN'S LAWS. !(a && b) is !a || !b - 'not both' means 'at least one is not'. !(a || b) is !a && !b - 'not either' means 'neither'. In both, the OPERATOR flips as well as the operands; that flip is the whole content of the law and it is what students drop.
THE DISPROOF. Take the row a = 0, b = 1. Then a && b is 0, so !(a && b) is 1. But !a is 1 and !b is 0, so !a && !b is 1 && 0 = 0. They disagree on that row, so !(a && b) is not !a && !b; the correct right-hand side is !a || !b. By symmetry they also disagree on a = 1, b = 0; they agree only on the two rows where a and b happen to be equal, which is why testing on tidy sample data does not expose the mistake.
WHY 0 < x < 10 IS ALWAYS TRUE. Relational operators associate left to right and C has no chained comparison, so the expression means (0 < x) < 10. The inner comparison is evaluated first and - by the integer rule - yields 1 or 0. That integer is then compared with 10, and both 1 and 0 are less than 10, so the whole expression evaluates to 1 for every possible value of x, including x = -500. The result does not depend on x at all, which is what makes the bug total rather than occasional.
WHAT TO WRITE INSTEAD: 0 < x && x < 10, i.e. two complete comparisons joined by &&. Each operand of && must be a full Boolean expression in its own right; a range test cannot be written by leaving one side of a comparison implicit. The same applies to if (x == 1 || 2), which means (x == 1) || 2 and is always true because 2 is nonzero - it must be x == 1 || x == 2.

questions.q: List the operators !, *, +, <, ==, &&, ||, = in order of precedence from highest to lowest, and use the list to bracket  x + 1 > y * 2 && !flag == 0  fully. Then explain what short-circuit evaluation guarantees for && and for ||, and why the order in which you write the two operands of && is part of the MEANING of the programme rather than a matter of style. End by saying what changes if && is replaced by &.
questions.concept: Precedence order, and short-circuiting as a rule about evaluation rather than about speed.
questions.why:
PRECEDENCE, highest first: ! (unary), then *, then +, then < (with <=, >, >=), then == (with !=), then &&, then ||, then = last of all. Two features are examined repeatedly: ! binds tighter than every comparison, and relational binds tighter than equality, which binds tighter than &&, which binds tighter than ||. Assignment is not a special form but an operator, and the lowest-precedence one here, which is why x = a > b assigns the comparison's value to x.
BRACKETING: ((x + 1) > (y * 2)) && ((!flag) == 0). Arithmetic forms first, giving x + 1 and y * 2; ! forms next, giving !flag; then > and == produce two truth values; then && joins them. Note what the right-hand half actually says: (!flag) == 0 is true exactly when !flag is 0, i.e. exactly when flag is true - so the whole clause is a long-winded way of writing flag, and anyone who read it as !(flag == 0) reached the same meaning by an argument that is wrong and will fail on the next example.
WHAT SHORT-CIRCUITING GUARANTEES. For a && b: a is evaluated first, and if a is false, b is not evaluated at all, since the result is already 0. For a || b: a is evaluated first, and if a is true, b is not evaluated, since the result is already 1. This is a guarantee of the language about what gets evaluated, not a permission the compiler may or may not take up.
WHY OPERAND ORDER IS MEANING. Because a skipped operand is never evaluated, its side effects never happen and any error it would have raised never occurs. So if (n != 0 && total / n > 5) is safe for n == 0 - the division is unreachable - while if (total / n > 5 && n != 0) performs the division first and divides by zero. The two have identical truth tables and different behaviour, which is only possible because evaluation is ordered. Likewise in i++ > 0 && j++ > 0, j is left untouched whenever the left operand is false, so the values of the variables afterwards depend on which operand was written first. The working rule: guard on the left, guarded expression on the right, and never hide an assignment, an increment or a call with an effect in the right-hand operand.
IF && BECOMES &. & is the bitwise and, a different operator: it combines the operands bit by bit and, critically, always evaluates both of them. The guard is therefore gone, and if (n != 0 & total / n > 5) divides by zero. It also gives different answers, because it works on bits rather than truths: 2 && 1 is 1, but 2 & 1 is 0. The single-character typo is invisible on the page and changes both what is computed and what is executed.

questions.q: For each of if, if-else, if-else-if, switch, while, do-while and for, state exactly when program control enters the body and the minimum and maximum number of times the body can run. For for, say which of its three parts runs only once and when the condition is tested relative to the increment. For switch, say what happens after a matching case finishes if there is no break. Finally, explain why if-else and two separate ifs are not interchangeable.
questions.concept: The entry condition and pass count of every control construct in the week.
questions.why:
if (c) S - control enters S only if c is true; the course's words are that program control will only move inside the if block if some conditions are satisfied, or else the entire block will be skipped. Body runs minimum 0, maximum 1 times.
if (c) S else T - if the condition is satisfied program control moves inside the if block, otherwise it moves to the else statement block. Exactly one of the two runs, always: there is no path on which both run and none on which neither runs.
if-else-if - used when more than two choices are integrated into the decision making process. Conditions are tested top to bottom and the FIRST TRUE ONE WINS; its branch runs and every remaining condition is skipped untested. At most one branch runs; if there is no final bare else and no condition is true, none runs. Each condition after the first is therefore read in the context of all the earlier ones having failed.
switch - we can execute one code block among many alternatives. The controlling expression is evaluated, control JUMPS to the matching case label, or to default if no label matches (and out of the switch entirely if there is no match and no default). After a matching case finishes with no break, control does not leave the switch: it falls straight through into the statements of the following case and continues doing so until it meets a break or the closing brace. So a missing break changes which code runs; it is not a formatting matter.
while (c) S - the condition is tested BEFORE the body; the loop iterates while the condition is true, and when the condition becomes false, program control passes to the line immediately following the loop. Body runs minimum 0, maximum unbounded.
do S while (c); - the body runs first and the condition is tested AFTER it, so it is guaranteed to execute at least one time: minimum 1, maximum unbounded.
for (init; c; inc) S - the init step is executed first, and ONLY ONCE; then the condition is evaluated, and if it is true the body executes, if false the body does not execute. After each pass the INCREMENT runs, and only then is the condition tested again. So the order per pass is condition, body, increment, condition - the increment happens after the body and before the next test, which is why the control variable holds the first FAILING value once the loop has ended. Body runs minimum 0, maximum unbounded.
goto - unconditional: control moves without checking any condition at all, so there is no entry condition to state.
WHY if-else AND TWO SEPARATE ifs DIFFER. With if (c) S else T, T runs precisely when c is false, the two branches are mutually exclusive by construction, and c is evaluated ONCE. With if (c) S followed by if (d) T, both conditions are evaluated independently, so if c and d are both true BOTH bodies run. Writing if (c) S then if (!c) T restores exclusivity but evaluates c twice, which differs if evaluating c has a side effect or if something between the two statements changes the value c depends on. The else is not shorthand for a second test; it is the guarantee that no second test is made.

checks.topic: The problems of improper integration: writing and evaluating the defining limit, applying the p-test arithmetic correctly at both ends, detecting an interior infinite discontinuity and splitting rather than applying the Fundamental Theorem across it, carrying out substitution and integration by parts inside a limit, and constructing comparisons by choosing the dominant-term comparison function, checking the direction of the inequality after taking reciprocals, and switching to limit comparison when the direct inequality points the wrong way.

questions.q: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^3) =
options: it diverges
questions.concept: p-test at infinity: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^p) = 1/(p - 1) for p > 1.
questions.why: Key (a): (integral from 1 to t of x^-3 dx) = [-1/(2x^2)] from 1 to t = 1/2 - 1/(2t^2) -> 1/2. (b) is 1/p, the commonest slip, since the value is 1/(p - 1) and not 1/p. (c) is the answer for p = 2 and shows the exponent being read off the antiderivative rather than the integrand. (d) applies the near-zero p-test at infinity.

questions.q: (integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-2x) dx) =
options: it diverges
questions.concept: (integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-kx) dx) = 1/k for k > 0.
questions.why: Key (b): (integral from 0 to t) = [-e^(-2x)/2] from 0 to t = 1/2 - e^(-2t)/2 -> 1/2, since e^(-2t) -> 0. (a) multiplies by the constant instead of dividing; the antiderivative of e^(-2x) is e^(-2x)/(-2), so the 2 lands in a denominator. (c) is the value for k = 1, ignoring the 2 altogether. (d) would require e^(-2t) to grow, which it does not; it is (integral from 0 to infinity of e^(+2x) dx) that diverges.

questions.q: (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^(2/3)) =
options: it diverges
questions.concept: p-test near zero: (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^p) converges for p < 1, to 1/(1 - p).
questions.why: Key (b): p = 2/3 < 1 and (integral from t to 1 of x^(-2/3) dx) = [3 x^(1/3)] from t to 1 = 3 - 3 t^(1/3) -> 3. (a) applies the infinity version of the p-test at the origin. (c) is 1/(1 - p) computed with p taken as 1/3. (d) is p itself. Note the antiderivative is x^(1/3)/(1/3) = 3 x^(1/3), and dropping the factor 3 is the arithmetic slip behind (d).

questions.q: (integral from 2 to infinity of dx/sqrt(x - 1)) =
options: it diverges
questions.concept: A shift does not affect convergence; p = 1/2 < 1 at infinity diverges.
questions.why: Key (d): (integral from 2 to t of (x-1)^(-1/2) dx) = [2 sqrt(x - 1)] from 2 to t = 2 sqrt(t - 1) - 2 -> infinity. (a) evaluates the antiderivative only at the lower limit, or assumes sqrt(t - 1) -> 0. (b) is the same error with the sign reversed. (c) uses the formula 1/(p - 1) with p = 1/2, ignoring that the formula only applies when p > 1; quoting a convergence formula is not a substitute for checking the convergence condition.

questions.q: (integral from -1 to 1 of dx/x^(4/3)) =
options: it diverges
questions.concept: An infinite discontinuity strictly inside the interval blocks the Fundamental Theorem; near zero p = 4/3 > 1 diverges.
questions.why: Key (d): (integral from 0 to 1 of x^(-4/3) dx) = lim as t -> 0+ of [-3 x^(-1/3)] from t to 1 = lim of (-3 + 3 t^(-1/3)) = +infinity, so the whole integral diverges. (a) is exactly the blind Fundamental Theorem answer, [-3 x^(-1/3)] from -1 to 1 = -3 - 3 = -6, and it is self-refuting because x^(-4/3) > 0 wherever defined. (b) is the same computation with a sign slip on (-1)^(-1/3). (c) appeals to symmetry as though two infinities could cancel. Compare (integral from -1 to 1 of dx/x^(2/3)), where p = 2/3 < 1 and the answer really is 6.

questions.q: (integral from 1 to infinity of (ln x)/x dx) =
options: 0, since (ln x)/x -> 0 as x -> infinity
it diverges
questions.concept: Substitution u = ln x turns this into (integral from 0 to infinity of u du), which diverges.
questions.why: Key (d): (integral from 1 to t) = [(ln x)^2/2] from 1 to t = (ln t)^2/2 -> infinity. (a) is the central misconception of the week: an integrand tending to 0 is not sufficient for convergence, exactly as 1/x -> 0 while its integral diverges. (b) is the value of (integral from 0 to 1 of u du), the right substitution with the wrong limits. (c) is the value of (integral from 1 to infinity of (ln x)/x^2 dx), a genuinely convergent neighbour; one extra power of x in the denominator flips the verdict.

questions.q: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/(x + e^x)):
options: converges, by comparison with e^(-x), since x + e^x > e^x on [1, infinity)
diverges, by comparison with 1/x, since 1/(x + e^x) < 1/x and (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x) diverges
converges, by comparison with 1/x, since 1/(x + e^x) < 1/x
diverges, because 1/(x + e^x) has no elementary antiderivative, so no finite value can exist
questions.concept: To prove convergence you must bound the integrand above by a convergent one; discarding the smaller term of the denominator makes the fraction larger.
questions.why: Key (a): for x >= 1, x + e^x > e^x > 0, so 0 < 1/(x + e^x) < e^(-x), and (integral from 1 to infinity of e^(-x) dx) = 1/e, finite. (b) and (c) both use the true but useless inequality 1/(x + e^x) < 1/x: being smaller than a divergent function is one of the two pairings the test says nothing about, so (b)'s conclusion is unjustified and (c)'s is right only by accident. (d) confuses 'no elementary antiderivative' with 'no value', when deciding convergence without evaluating is the entire point of the test.

questions.q: (integral from 1 to infinity of (sqrt(x) + 1)/(x^2 + 3) dx):
options: converges: limit comparison with 1/x^(3/2) gives L = 1
diverges: comparison with 1/sqrt(x), which the integrand is smaller than
converges: direct comparison with 1/x^2, since the denominator has degree 2
diverges: limit comparison with 1/x gives L = 1
questions.concept: Keep the leading terms to choose the comparison function, then use limit comparison when the direct inequality misbehaves.
questions.why: Key (a): the integrand behaves like x^(1/2)/x^2 = x^(-3/2), and the ratio to x^(-3/2) is (x^2 + x^(3/2))/(x^2 + 3) -> 1, with 0 < 1 < infinity, so both integrals do the same thing; (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^(3/2)) converges. (b) uses an inequality in the direction that proves nothing, since 1/sqrt(x) is divergent at infinity. (c) asserts a false inequality: the ratio to 1/x^2 tends to infinity, so the integrand is eventually LARGER than 1/x^2, which is why limit comparison is needed. (d) miscomputes the limit, which is 0 rather than 1, and L = 0 against a divergent g yields no conclusion in any case.

questions.q: (explain why) Evaluate, showing the limit at every stage: (i) (integral from 0 to infinity of dx/(1 + x^2)); (ii) (integral from 0 to infinity of x dx/(1 + x^2)); (iii) (integral from 0 to infinity of x dx/(1 + x^2)^2). Then say in one sentence what single feature separates the divergent one from the convergent ones.
questions.concept: The order of decay of the integrand, not the presence of an x in the numerator, decides convergence at infinity, and every claim must be made through an explicit limit.
questions.why: (i) lim as t -> infinity of [arctan x] from 0 to t = lim of (arctan t - 0) = pi/2, convergent. (ii) substitute u = 1 + x^2, du = 2x dx, so (integral from 0 to t) = [(1/2) ln(1 + x^2)] from 0 to t = (1/2) ln(1 + t^2) -> infinity, divergent. (iii) the same substitution gives (integral from 0 to t) = [-(1/2)(1 + x^2)^(-1)] from 0 to t = 1/2 - 1/(2(1 + t^2)) -> 1/2, convergent; equivalently (1/2)(integral from 1 to infinity of du/u^2) = 1/2. The separating feature is the order of decay: in (i) the integrand is of order x^(-2) and in (iii) of order x^(-3), both faster than x^(-1), whereas in (ii) it is x/x^2, of order x^(-1) exactly, the boundary case p = 1, which always diverges. The x in the numerator is not itself the problem, since (iii) has the same numerator and converges; the problem is that in (ii) it cancels one power from the denominator.

questions.q: (explain why) Show that (integral from 1 to infinity of e^(-x^2) dx) converges. State the inequality you use, the interval on which it holds and why it holds there, evaluate the comparison integral in full, and state precisely what has and has not been proved about the original integral.
questions.concept: Comparison decides convergence for integrands with no elementary antiderivative, and concludes convergence only, never a value.
questions.why: e^(-x^2) has no elementary antiderivative, so evaluation is unavailable and comparison is the only route. Inequality: for x >= 1 we have x^2 >= x, hence -x^2 <= -x, hence 0 < e^(-x^2) <= e^(-x), using that e^t is increasing. The interval matters: on (0, 1) the inequality reverses because there x^2 < x, but convergence depends only on the tail so an eventual inequality suffices, and here the integral starts at 1 in any case. Comparison integral: (integral from 1 to infinity of e^(-x) dx) = lim as t -> infinity of [-e^(-x)] from 1 to t = lim of (e^(-1) - e^(-t)) = 1/e, finite. Both functions are non-negative and continuous on [1, infinity), so the Comparison Test applies in its convergent direction and (integral from 1 to infinity of e^(-x^2) dx) CONVERGES. What has not been proved is any value: the argument gives only the bound 0 < (integral) <= 1/e, and writing '= 1/e' would be wrong.

questions.q: (explain why) Decide whether (integral from 0 to infinity of dx/(sqrt(x)(1 + x))) converges. Explain why the integral must be split before any test is applied, and treat each piece separately with a named comparison and a p-test.
questions.concept: An integral improper at two places must be split, because the limit definition handles one bad point at a time, and each end may need a different comparison and a different p-test.
questions.why: The integrand is unbounded as x -> 0+ (Type II there) and the interval runs to infinity (Type I there), and the limit definition handles exactly one problem point per limit, so write (integral from 0 to infinity) = (integral from 0 to 1) + (integral from 1 to infinity); any interior split point does. Near 0: on (0, 1], 1 + x >= 1, so 0 < 1/(sqrt(x)(1 + x)) <= 1/sqrt(x), and (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^(1/2)) has p = 1/2 < 1 and converges, to 2; by comparison the first piece converges. Near infinity: on [1, infinity), 1 + x > x so sqrt(x)(1 + x) > x^(3/2), hence 0 < 1/(sqrt(x)(1 + x)) < 1/x^(3/2), and (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^(3/2)) has p = 3/2 > 1 and converges, to 2; by comparison the second piece converges. Both halves converge, so the whole integral CONVERGES. Note that the two p-tests point opposite ways, p = 1/2 saving the left end and p = 3/2 the right, which is exactly why a single test applied to the whole range would be meaningless. For completeness u = sqrt(x) gives the value pi, but convergence was all that was asked.

questions.q: (explain why) Evaluate (integral from 0 to 2 of dx/(x - 1)^(2/3)), showing every limit, and then explain why (integral from 0 to 2 of dx/(x - 1)^(4/3)) diverges even though the two integrands differ only in an exponent.
questions.concept: An interior infinite discontinuity forces a split into two one-sided limits, and the p-test near the singularity, where p < 1 converges, decides each piece.
questions.why: The integrand is undefined at x = 1, inside [0, 2], so (integral from 0 to 2) = lim as t -> 1- of (integral from 0 to t) + lim as s -> 1+ of (integral from s to 2). An antiderivative is 3 (x - 1)^(1/3), which is defined for negative arguments since cube roots of negatives exist. Left piece: lim as t -> 1- of [3(x-1)^(1/3)] from 0 to t = 0 - 3(-1)^(1/3) = 0 - 3(-1) = 3. Right piece: lim as s -> 1+ of [3(x-1)^(1/3)] from s to 2 = 3(1)^(1/3) - 0 = 3. Both converge, so the value is 3 + 3 = 6. For (x - 1)^(-4/3) the exponent near the singularity is p = 4/3 > 1, which fails the near-singularity p-test: an antiderivative is -3(x-1)^(-1/3), and lim as s -> 1+ of (integral from s to 2) = lim of (-3 + 3(s - 1)^(-1/3)) = +infinity. One divergent piece is enough, so that integral DIVERGES. The difference between 2/3 and 4/3 is the difference between a spike that is integrable and one that is not: near the bad point the integrand must blow up more slowly than 1/(x - 1) for the area to stay finite. Applying the Fundamental Theorem straight through would give [-3(x-1)^(-1/3)] from 0 to 2 = -3 - 3 = -6, a negative number for a positive integrand, which is the visible sign that the interior singularity was missed.

checks.topic: Numerical Lorentz-force work: computing q*v*B*sin(theta) and qE and combining them as vectors rather than as numbers, showing the magnetic force does zero work, evaluating the orbit radius r = mv/(qB) and period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) and the helical pitch, applying F = B*I*L*sin(theta) with the length converted to metres and the angle taken from the current, finding the selector speed v = E/B, converting gauss to tesla, and getting wavelength and photon energy from c = f*lambda and E = h*f, with the unit, angle, sign and direction traps at each step

questions.q: A charge q = +4.0 microcoulomb moves at v = 2.5x10^5 m/s, its velocity making 30 degrees with a uniform magnetic field B = 0.60 T, and a uniform electric field of magnitude E = 1.2x10^3 V/m is present in the same region. The magnitude of the magnetic force on the charge is:
questions.concept: F = q*v*B*sin(theta), theta between v and B
questions.why: q*v = (4.0x10^-6)(2.5x10^5) = 1.0; times B = 0.60; times sin(30 degrees) = 0.500 gives 0.30 N. (a) 0.60 N ignores the angle, the value that applies only when v is perpendicular to B. (c) 0.52 N is q*v*B*cos(30 degrees), the sin/cos swap. (d) 1.0 N is q*v with B dropped entirely, and its units are not newtons.
